name: Paracetamol
used_for: Relieves pain such as headaches, toothache, sore throat and joint pain, and brings down a high temperature (fever), for example with a cold or flu.
how_it_works: It changes the way your body senses pain and helps cool the body down.
how_to_take: Can be taken with or without food. Leave at least 4 hours between doses and take no more than 4 doses in 24 hours. Do not take it for more than 3 days unless a doctor tells you to. Always check the dose on the pack.
common_side_effects: Side effects are very rare when taken at the right dose
serious_warnings: If you have taken more than the pack says, get urgent medical help even if you feel well - too much can damage your liver
Yellow skin or whites of the eyes, or feeling sick (possible liver problem) - contact a doctor
Bruising easily or nosebleeds - contact a doctor
Swollen throat or tongue, itchy raised rash, or trouble breathing (allergic reaction) - get emergency help
avoid: Other medicines that also contain paracetamol, such as cold and flu remedies (risk of taking too much)
Ask a doctor first if you drink heavily, or have liver or kidney problems
Check with a pharmacist if you take anti-sickness medicines (such as domperidone) or blood thinners (such as warfarin)

name: Ibuprofen
used_for: Relieves pain (such as headaches, period pain, toothache, and joint or muscle pain), reduces swelling and brings down a fever.
how_it_works: It stops the body making a substance that causes pain, fever and swelling.
how_to_take: Take with or after food and swallow tablets whole with water. Leave at least 4 hours between doses. Do not take it for more than 10 days unless a doctor says so.
serious_warnings: Black, sticky poo, vomiting blood, or tummy pain with pale skin (bleeding or ulcer in the stomach) - get urgent help
Blood in your pee, or swollen ankles, feet or hands (possible kidney problem) - contact a doctor
Swollen throat or tongue, itchy raised rash, or trouble breathing (allergic reaction) - get emergency help
avoid: Other NSAID painkillers such as aspirin, diclofenac or naproxen at the same time
Drinking a lot of alcohol
Check with a doctor or pharmacist if you take blood thinners (such as warfarin), steroids, antidepressants or blood pressure medicines
Ask a doctor first if you have asthma, a stomach ulcer, heart, liver or kidney problems, or are pregnant

name: Diclofenac
used_for: Relieves pain and swelling, for example from arthritis, sprains, back pain, migraine or after dental surgery.
how_it_works: It reduces hormones in the body that cause pain and swelling.
how_to_take: Take with a meal or snack, just after eating, or with a drink of milk. Swallow tablets whole; do not crush, break or chew them. Use the lowest dose for the shortest time.
serious_warnings: Black poo or vomiting blood (bleeding in the stomach or gut) - get urgent help
Severe indigestion, heartburn or stomach pain - contact a doctor
Yellow skin or whites of the eyes (possible liver problem) - contact a doctor
Breathlessness, tiredness and swollen legs or ankles (possible heart problem) - contact a doctor
Chest pain, or sudden weakness on one side of the body or trouble speaking - call emergency services
Swollen lips, mouth or throat, or trouble breathing (allergic reaction) - get emergency help
avoid: Other NSAID painkillers such as aspirin, ibuprofen or naproxen, unless a doctor says so
Drinking too much alcohol (it can irritate the stomach)
Check with a doctor if you take blood thinners (such as warfarin), blood pressure medicines, steroids, some antidepressants or some antibiotics
Ask a doctor first if you have asthma, stomach ulcers, high blood pressure, heart, liver or kidney disease, or are pregnant

name: Chlorzoxazone
used_for: Relieves pain and stiffness from muscle strains and sprains. It is used together with rest, physiotherapy and painkillers.
how_to_take: Usually taken 3 or 4 times a day, exactly as prescribed. It can make you drowsy, so be careful until you know how it affects you.
serious_warnings: Yellow skin or eyes - call your doctor straight away
Skin rash or itching - call your doctor straight away
Stomach pain - call your doctor straight away
Collapse, a fit, trouble breathing or cannot be woken (possible overdose) - call emergency services
avoid: Alcohol, which can make side effects worse
Driving or using machines until you know how it affects you
Tell your doctor if you have liver disease
People aged 65 or over should ask their doctor about the risks, as it is not usually advised for older adults
notes: Urine may turn purple or red; this is harmless. The source does not explain how it works, so no explanation is given.

name: Serratiopeptidase
notes: No information in trusted sources (not an approved medicine in the UK or US). App should say: limited reliable information is available for this ingredient; please ask your pharmacist or doctor.

name: Metformin
used_for: Lowers blood sugar in type 2 diabetes. It can be used on its own or with other diabetes medicines.
how_it_works: It lowers the level of sugar in your blood.
how_to_take: Take with food, usually 1 to 3 times a day. Swallow tablets whole with water; do not crush or chew them. Keep taking it - if you stop, your blood sugar may rise again.
common_side_effects: A change in the way things taste
Low vitamin B12, which can make you feel very tired
serious_warnings: Being sick, stomach pain, muscle cramps, breathing problems or feeling extremely tired (too much acid in the blood, rare) - call emergency services
Yellow skin or whites of the eyes (liver problem) - contact a doctor
Swollen throat or tongue, itchy raised rash, or trouble breathing (allergic reaction) - call emergency services
avoid: Drinking a lot of alcohol
If you are being sick, have diarrhoea or a fever, you may get dehydrated - talk to a pharmacist or doctor
Check with a doctor if you take NSAID painkillers (such as ibuprofen or diclofenac), water tablets (diuretics) or some blood pressure medicines

name: Glimepiride
used_for: Lowers blood sugar in type 2 diabetes, along with diet and exercise.
how_it_works: It helps your pancreas make insulin and helps your body use insulin better, which lowers blood sugar.
how_to_take: Usually taken once a day with breakfast or the first main meal of the day, at about the same time each day. Keep taking it even if you feel well.
common_side_effects: Changes in blood sugar (it can make blood sugar too low)
serious_warnings: Shaking, sweating, hunger, a fast heartbeat, headache or unclear thinking (low blood sugar) - have juice, a sugary drink or food straight away
Someone with low blood sugar who has a fit, faints or cannot be woken - call emergency services
Yellow skin or eyes, pale poo, dark urine or pain in the upper right of the stomach - call your doctor straight away
Unusual bruising or bleeding, fever or a sore throat - call your doctor straight away
avoid: Alcohol, which can make side effects worse
Too much sun - it can make your skin more sensitive, so use sunscreen and cover up
Starting aspirin or NSAID painkillers (such as ibuprofen) without asking your doctor
People aged 65 or over should ask their doctor about the risks, as it is not usually advised for older adults

name: Amlodipine
used_for: Treats high blood pressure (lowering the risk of heart attack and stroke) and prevents chest pain caused by angina.
how_it_works: It relaxes and widens your blood vessels, so blood can be pumped around your body more easily.
how_to_take: Take once a day at the same time, before or after food. Most people need it long term. Do not stop taking it unless a doctor tells you to - stopping suddenly can be dangerous.
serious_warnings: Sudden, severe tummy pain that does not go away (inflamed pancreas) - get urgent help
Blistering or peeling skin, or painful sores with flu-like symptoms (serious skin reaction) - get urgent help
Chest pain (a heart attack is very rare) - call emergency services
Swollen throat or tongue, itchy raised rash, or trouble breathing (allergic reaction) - get emergency help
avoid: Grapefruit and grapefruit juice
Drinking a lot of alcohol (it can make your blood pressure too low)
Check with a doctor if you take other blood pressure medicines, simvastatin, some antibiotics or antifungal medicines, or St John's wort

name: Telmisartan
used_for: Treats high blood pressure. It also lowers the chance of heart attack and stroke in people aged 55 or over who are at high risk.
how_it_works: It blocks natural substances that tighten your blood vessels, so blood flows more smoothly and the heart pumps more easily.
how_to_take: Take once a day at the same time, with or without food. Keep the tablet in its blister pack until you take it. Keep taking it even if you feel well.
common_side_effects: Sinus pain or a blocked nose
serious_warnings: Swelling of the face, lips, tongue, throat, eyes, hands, feet or legs - call your doctor straight away
Hoarseness, or trouble breathing or swallowing - call your doctor straight away
Blistering skin or a rash - call your doctor straight away
Fainting - contact your doctor
Do not take it if you are pregnant. If you become pregnant, contact your doctor straight away
avoid: Aspirin and NSAID painkillers such as ibuprofen or diclofenac, unless your doctor agrees
Potassium supplements, or salt substitutes that contain potassium, unless your doctor agrees
Driving or using machines until you know if it makes you dizzy

name: Atorvastatin
used_for: Lowers cholesterol and helps prevent angina, heart attacks and strokes.
how_it_works: It slows down how much cholesterol your body makes.
how_to_take: Take once a day at the same time, with or without food. Swallow tablets whole with water. You usually need it for a long time, sometimes for life.
common_side_effects: Blocked or runny nose, or nosebleeds
serious_warnings: Muscle cramps, severe pain or weakness, sometimes with a fever or red or brown pee - contact a doctor straight away
Yellow skin or whites of the eyes (liver problem) - contact a doctor
Severe stomach pain (inflamed pancreas) - contact a doctor
Swollen throat or tongue, itchy raised rash, or trouble breathing (allergic reaction) - get emergency help
avoid: More than 1 or 2 small glasses of grapefruit juice a day
Drinking a lot of alcohol (it raises the risk of liver problems)
Taking it in pregnancy - tell your doctor if you are pregnant or trying to get pregnant
Check with a doctor if you take other cholesterol medicines, some antibiotics (such as clarithromycin or erythromycin), antifungal medicines, warfarin or St John's wort

name: Rosuvastatin
used_for: Lowers cholesterol and helps prevent angina, heart attacks and strokes.
how_it_works: It slows down how much cholesterol your body makes.
how_to_take: Take once a day at the same time, with or without food. Swallow tablets whole with a drink of water. You usually need it for a long time, sometimes for life.
serious_warnings: Muscle cramps, severe pain or weakness, sometimes with a fever or red or brown pee - contact a doctor straight away
Yellow skin or whites of the eyes (liver problem) - contact a doctor
Severe stomach pain (inflamed pancreas) - contact a doctor
Swollen throat or tongue, itchy raised rash, or trouble breathing (allergic reaction) - get emergency help
avoid: Drinking a lot of alcohol (it raises the risk of liver problems)
Taking it in pregnancy - tell your doctor if you are pregnant or trying to get pregnant
Check with a doctor if you take other cholesterol medicines, some antibiotics (such as erythromycin), blood thinners (such as warfarin or clopidogrel) or the combined contraceptive pill

name: Levothyroxine
used_for: Treats an underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism), helping with symptoms like tiredness, weight gain and low mood.
how_it_works: It replaces the thyroid hormone your body normally makes.
how_to_take: Take once a day on an empty stomach, 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast, tea or coffee, or any other medicine. Take it at the same time each day and swallow it with a glass of water. Most people take it for life, with regular blood tests to check the dose.
serious_warnings: High temperature, fast or irregular heartbeat, feeling dizzy or faint, or yellow skin or eyes (thyroid crisis) - get urgent help
Swollen throat or tongue, itchy raised rash, or trouble breathing (allergic reaction) - get emergency help
avoid: Calcium or iron supplements, antacids and other indigestion medicines at the same time - ask your pharmacist how far apart to take them
Stomach acid medicines such as omeprazole - tell your doctor
Food, tea or coffee within 30 to 60 minutes after your dose
Tell your doctor if you take epilepsy medicines, antidepressants, heart medicines, St John's wort or biotin
notes: Most side effects happen when the dose is too high and often improve when the dose is changed.

name: Pantoprazole
used_for: Reduces stomach acid. Treats heartburn, acid reflux and stomach ulcers, and helps prevent stomach ulcers.
how_it_works: It stops the 'proton pumps' in your stomach lining from working properly, so your stomach makes less acid.
how_to_take: Usually taken once a day, first thing in the morning, about 1 hour before a meal. Swallow whole with a drink of water. You should feel better in 2 to 3 days, but it can take up to 4 weeks to work fully.
common_side_effects: Most people have no side effects
serious_warnings: Joint pain with a red rash on skin exposed to the sun - contact a doctor
Stomach pain that gets worse, yellow skin or eyes, or dark pee (liver problem) - contact a doctor
Pain when peeing, peeing less, lower back pain, swollen ankles, rash or fever (kidney problem) - contact a doctor
Severe diarrhoea, or diarrhoea that does not stop - contact a doctor
Swollen lips, mouth or throat, or trouble breathing (allergic reaction) - call emergency services
avoid: Taking it for more than 4 weeks without a doctor's advice, if you bought it yourself
Rich, spicy or fatty foods, caffeine and alcohol, which can make symptoms worse
St John's wort
Check with a doctor if you take warfarin, methotrexate, or antifungal or HIV medicines
It is not usually recommended in pregnancy - tell your doctor

name: Omeprazole
used_for: Reduces stomach acid. Treats heartburn, acid reflux (GORD) and stomach ulcers.
how_it_works: It lowers the amount of acid your stomach makes.
how_to_take: Usually taken once a day in the morning (or morning and evening if taken twice a day), with or without food. Swallow with water; do not chew or crush capsules.
serious_warnings: Tiredness, dizziness, muscle twitches or weakness (very low vitamin B12) - contact a doctor
A rash on skin exposed to the sun, with joint pain - contact a doctor
Bones that break more easily, especially with long-term use - talk to your doctor
Swollen throat or tongue, itchy raised rash, or trouble breathing (allergic reaction) - get emergency help
avoid: Alcohol, which can increase stomach acid
Taking it for more than 2 weeks without a doctor, if you bought it yourself
Other stomach acid medicines such as famotidine, unless your doctor agrees
Check with a doctor if you take warfarin, clopidogrel, digoxin, diazepam, phenytoin or St John's wort

name: Esomeprazole
used_for: Reduces stomach acid. Treats heartburn, acid reflux and stomach ulcers.
how_it_works: It stops the 'proton pumps' in your stomach lining from working properly, so your stomach makes less acid.
how_to_take: Usually taken once a day, first thing in the morning, with or without food. Swallow whole with a drink of still water; do not chew or crush.
serious_warnings: Yellow skin, pale poo, dark pee and feeling more tired than usual (liver problem) - contact a doctor
Joint pain with a red rash on skin exposed to the sun - contact a doctor
Severe diarrhoea, or diarrhoea that does not stop - contact a doctor
Swollen lips, mouth or throat, or trouble breathing (allergic reaction) - call emergency services
avoid: Alcohol, and rich, spicy or fatty food, which can make symptoms worse
St John's wort
Check with a doctor if you take clopidogrel, warfarin, digoxin, antifungal medicines or some antidepressants
It is not recommended in pregnancy - tell your doctor

name: Domperidone
used_for: Relieves feeling sick (nausea) and being sick (vomiting).
how_it_works: It tightens the muscles at the top of your stomach and relaxes those at the bottom, and blocks signals to the part of the brain that makes you sick.
how_to_take: Take before meals. Swallow whole with water; do not crush or chew. It is usually only for a short time (up to 1 week).
serious_warnings: A fast or irregular heartbeat, or a fit (seizure) - call emergency services
Muscles or eyes moving in an unusual way you cannot control - contact a doctor
Problems peeing - contact a doctor
Swollen lips, mouth or throat, or trouble breathing (allergic reaction) - call emergency services
avoid: Alcohol, which can make side effects like sleepiness or an irregular heartbeat worse
Taking it for longer than prescribed
Check with a doctor if you take antibiotics, antifungal medicines, antidepressants, or heart or blood pressure medicines
Taking more than one anti-sickness medicine at a time
It may not be suitable if you are over 60, or have heart, liver or kidney problems - ask your doctor

name: Famotidine
used_for: Reduces stomach acid. Treats ulcers, acid reflux and heartburn.
how_it_works: It lowers the amount of acid your stomach makes.
how_to_take: Take as prescribed - often once a day at bedtime, or two to four times a day. Swallow tablets with a full glass of water.
serious_warnings: Hives, rash or itching - call your doctor straight away
Swelling of the face, throat, tongue, lips, eyes, hands, feet or legs - call your doctor straight away
Hoarseness, or trouble breathing or swallowing - get emergency help
avoid: Other heartburn medicines, unless your doctor agrees
Tell your doctor if you have kidney disease

name: Amoxicillin
used_for: Treats bacterial infections, such as chest, throat, dental and skin infections.
how_it_works: It kills the bacteria that cause the infection.
how_to_take: Take before or after food, with doses spaced evenly through the day (for example morning, mid-afternoon and bedtime). Swallow capsules whole with water. Finish the whole course even if you feel better.
serious_warnings: Diarrhoea with blood or mucus, or severe diarrhoea - stop and call a doctor
Pale poo, dark pee, or yellow skin or eyes - stop and call a doctor
A rash with round red patches and a high temperature - stop and call a doctor
Swollen lips, mouth or throat, a widespread rash, or trouble breathing (serious allergic reaction) - call emergency services
avoid: Do not take it if you are allergic to penicillin - tell your doctor about any allergy
Tell your doctor if you take warfarin or methotrexate
Tell your doctor if you have glandular fever

name: Azithromycin
used_for: Treats bacterial infections, such as chest, ear, throat and skin infections.
how_it_works: It kills the bacteria that cause the infection.
how_to_take: Usually taken once a day at the same time, often for a short course. Take tablets or capsules at least 1 hour before food or 2 hours after eating, and swallow them whole with water. Finish the whole course even if you feel better.
common_side_effects: Changes to your sense of taste
serious_warnings: Fast or irregular heartbeat - call a doctor now
Yellow skin or eyes, or pale poo with dark pee - call a doctor now
Ringing in the ears, hearing loss or feeling unsteady - call a doctor now
Severe stomach or back pain - call a doctor now
Peeing more or less than usual, or blood in your pee - call a doctor now
Severe diarrhoea, or diarrhoea with blood or mucus - call a doctor now
Chest pain - call emergency services
Swollen lips, mouth or throat, or trouble breathing (allergic reaction) - call emergency services
avoid: Antacids: take azithromycin at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after them
Alcohol, if it makes you dizzy
Tell your doctor if you have heart rhythm problems or myasthenia gravis
Check with a doctor if you take medicines that affect your heartbeat (such as domperidone), blood thinners, statins (such as atorvastatin) or digoxin

name: Cetirizine
used_for: Relieves allergy symptoms such as sneezing, runny nose, itchy watery eyes, and itchy skin rashes or hives.
how_it_works: It blocks histamine, a chemical your body makes during an allergic reaction that causes itching, sneezing and watery eyes.
how_to_take: Take once a day, with or without food. Swallow tablets whole with a drink of water.
serious_warnings: Bruising more easily, or bleeding that takes longer to stop - contact a doctor
Swollen lips, mouth or throat, or trouble breathing (allergic reaction) - call emergency services
avoid: Alcohol, which can make you sleepy
Driving or cycling if it makes you sleepy
Other medicines that make you drowsy, give you a dry mouth or make it hard to pee - check with a pharmacist
Tell your doctor if you have kidney failure, epilepsy, or trouble peeing

name: Levocetirizine
used_for: Relieves allergy symptoms such as sneezing, runny nose, itchy watery eyes, and hives.
how_it_works: It blocks the action of histamine, a substance in the body that causes allergy symptoms.
how_to_take: Take once a day in the evening, with or without food, at the same time every day.
serious_warnings: Hives, rash or itching - call your doctor straight away
Swelling of the arms, hands, feet, ankles or lower legs - call your doctor straight away
Severe itching a few days after stopping, if you took it for months or years - talk to your doctor
avoid: Alcohol, which can add to drowsiness
Driving or using machines until you know how it affects you
Tell your doctor if you have kidney disease
Do not breastfeed while taking it

name: Aspirin
used_for: Low-dose aspirin helps prevent blood clots, lowering the chance of a heart attack or stroke.
how_it_works: It blocks natural substances in the body that cause blood clots, pain and swelling.
how_to_take: Low-dose aspirin is usually taken as 1 tablet once a day. Swallow gastro-resistant tablets whole with a glass of water. It is often taken for a long time, sometimes for life.
common_side_effects: Bleeding more easily than usual (cuts take longer to stop bleeding)
serious_warnings: Tummy pain, pale skin, vomiting blood, or black, sticky poo (bleeding in the stomach) - get urgent help
Shortness of breath or wheezing - get urgent help
Swollen throat or tongue, itchy raised rash, or trouble breathing (allergic reaction) - get emergency help
avoid: Other NSAID painkillers such as ibuprofen or naproxen, unless your doctor agrees
Too much alcohol (it raises the risk of side effects)
Check with a doctor if you take blood thinners (such as warfarin), steroids, some antidepressants, some blood pressure medicines or methotrexate
Do not give aspirin to children aged 15 or under

name: Vitamin D3 (Colecalciferol)
used_for: Treats and prevents low vitamin D. Vitamin D helps the body take in calcium for strong bones.
how_it_works: It helps your body take in more calcium and phosphorus from food, and helps your kidneys keep calcium in the body.
how_to_take: Take exactly as your doctor says. High-strength doses are usually taken once a week for a few weeks, not every day. Swallow capsules whole with water, with your main meal of the day.
serious_warnings: Needing to pee more often - contact a doctor
Swelling in any part of the body - contact a doctor
A high temperature with sharp pain in your side or lower back (possible kidney stones) - contact a doctor
Being sick, confusion, bone or joint pain, or an irregular heartbeat (too much calcium) - contact a doctor
Swollen lips, mouth or throat, or trouble breathing (allergic reaction) - call emergency services
avoid: Other supplements that contain vitamin D or calcium, unless your doctor agrees
Taking more than prescribed
Tell your doctor if you take digoxin, water tablets (diuretics) or steroids
Tell your doctor if you have kidney problems or have had kidney stones

name: Calcium (carbonate)
used_for: A supplement when you do not get enough calcium from food. Calcium is needed for healthy bones, muscles, nerves and heart. Calcium carbonate is also used as an antacid for heartburn.
how_it_works: It adds calcium to your body when your diet does not have enough.
how_to_take: As a supplement, take it with food or just after meals, with a full glass of water. Chew chewable tablets well before swallowing. Follow the dose on the pack or from your doctor.
serious_warnings: Being sick, confusion, bone or joint pain, or an irregular heartbeat (too much calcium) - contact a doctor
Collapse, a fit, trouble breathing or cannot be woken (possible overdose) - call emergency services
avoid: Taking it within 1 to 2 hours of other medicines - calcium can make them work less well (for example thyroid medicine)
Tell your doctor if you have kidney disease or stomach problems
